video_caption: The video segment begins with a title slide featuring the text "ENDOCRINE SYSTEM" in green, along with the objective: "List the major endocrine organs and the hormones they secrete. Then for each hormone discuss its effects on target cells." Below this, a book cover titled "Anatomy and Physiology" in orange and gray is displayed. The next frame shows a white line drawing of a human body, highlighting and labeling various endocrine glands including the Pineal gland, Pituitary gland, Thyroid, Thymus, Adrenal glands, Pancreas, Uterus, Ovaries (female), and Testes (male). Two magnified insets provide closer views of the brain's endocrine structures (Pineal gland, Thalamus, Pituitary gland) and the Thyroid gland (Thyroid cartilage of the larynx, Thyroid gland, Parathyroid glands, Trachea). A gray arrow points from the thyroid in the main figure to its magnified inset. The final frame focuses on "THE ENDOCRINE PANCREAS" with a detailed diagram showing the pancreas, duodenum, spleen, splenic artery, bile duct (from gall bladder), common bile duct, and pancreatic duct. Labels indicate "Pancreatic hormones: * Insulin * Glucagon", "Pancreatic islets" (small green circles), and "Acinar cells secrete digestive enzymes" (small blue circles). An inset provides a microscopic view of a "Pancreatic islet" further detailing "Alpha cells", "Beta cells", and "Exocrine acinus". All slides have a white background with a colorful striped border (green, orange, red, blue, yellow) and the "openstax™" logo.

The video segment displays a detailed anatomical illustration titled "THE ENDOCRINE PANCREAS," with an OpenStax logo in the top right corner. The main image shows a light brown, elongated pancreas situated near the duodenum of the small intestine (pink, C-shaped structure on the left). Connected to the duodenum are the common bile duct and a bile duct from the gallbladder. Running along the top edge of the pancreas is the splenic artery, which leads to the spleen (dark purple, kidney-bean-shaped organ on the right). Within the pancreas, green ducts represent the pancreatic duct system, and several small, yellow-orange, circular structures are labeled "Pancreatic islets." A text box above the pancreas notes "Pancreatic hormones: * Insulin * Glucagon." The bulk of the pancreatic tissue consists of "Acinar cells secret[ing] digestive enzymes," indicated by various small circular clusters throughout the organ, some with yellow highlights suggesting enzyme production, and these enzymes flow into the pancreatic duct. A square outline on one of the pancreatic islets points to a magnified inset image. This inset shows a pink-stained micrograph of a "Pancreatic islet," identifying "Alpha cells" and "Beta cells" within the islet, surrounded by "Exocrine acinus" tissue. The overall scene provides a comprehensive view of the pancreas, highlighting both its exocrine (digestive enzymes) and endocrine (hormone production in islets) functions.

The video displays a static informational graphic titled "THE ENDOCRINE PANCREAS" in green text on a white background with a colorful striped border. The OpenStax logo is visible in the top right corner. The main illustration shows an anatomical diagram of the pancreas, a yellowish organ, situated behind the pink duodenum of the small intestine and connected to the reddish-purple spleen on the left. Various structures are labeled: the Splenic artery (red vessel), Pancreatic islets (small yellow clusters), Pancreatic duct (green tube), Bile duct and Common bile duct (green tubes near the duodenum), and Acinar cells (pinkish-purple surrounding tissue) that secrete digestive enzymes (represented by orange dots). A purple text box indicates "Pancreatic hormones: • Insulin • Glucagon," with lines pointing to the pancreatic islets. An enlarged inset on the bottom right shows a microscopic view of a "Pancreatic islet," highlighting "Alpha cells," "Beta cells," and surrounding "Exocrine acinus" cells within the pink-stained tissue. The speaker describes how pancreatic islets, also known as islets of Langerhans, contain alpha cells that produce glucagon and beta cells that produce insulin, which together regulate blood glucose concentration.

The video displays three microscopic images of pancreatic tissue, starting with a low magnification view labeled "Pancreas 40X" (0:01). This initial image, stained purple, clearly shows various components: darker, abundant "Acini cells" (exocrine cells), lighter, circular "Islets of Langerhans" (endocrine cells), and "Pancreatic ducts" embedded within connective tissue. The speaker highlights these features, explaining that acini cells are exocrine and islets are endocrine structures. The video then transitions to a higher magnification view, labeled "Pancreas 100X" (0:24), providing more detail of the same structures, with arrows pointing to "Islets of Langerhans" (one outlined by a dotted circle), "Pancreatic duct," and "Acini cells." Finally, a "Pancreas 400X" image (0:36) focuses on a single islet, heavily outlined by a dotted circle and labeled "Islets of Langerhans," showing individual cells and nuclei within, surrounded by the darker "Acini cells" and with a "Pancreatic duct" visible in the upper right. The speaker details the endocrine cells within the islet, mentioning alpha cells (producing glucagon) and beta cells (producing insulin). The video ends with a repeat of the 100X magnification view (0:55), again labeling "Islets of Langerhans" and "Acini cells." The overall progression is from a broad histological overview to a detailed cellular view of the pancreatic islet.

The video displays two microscopic views of a pancreas tissue slide. The first image, labeled "Pancreas 100X," shows a field of purplish-pink stained cells. Two distinct, lighter-stained, somewhat circular clusters of cells are labeled "Islets of Langerhans" with white arrows pointing to them, representing the endocrine portion of the pancreas. The surrounding, darker-stained cells are labeled "Acini cells," indicating the exocrine part responsible for digestive enzyme production. The video then transitions to a higher magnification view, labeled "Pancreas 400X," focusing on one of the islets. This "Islets of Langerhans" is outlined by a white dashed line, revealing numerous individual cell nuclei as small, dark purple dots, and several lighter, elongated areas which are blood vessels, contributing to the lighter staining of the region. To the upper left of the islet, two smaller, darker-stained clusters are highlighted by dashed circles and again labeled "Acini cells," which appear more densely packed and granular than the islet cells.

The video segment presents an educational infographic titled "THE ENDOCRINE PANCREAS" with the OpenStax logo displayed in the top right corner against a colorful striped background. The infographic illustrates the regulation of blood glucose. It begins with a central image of a finger pricking a blood glucose meter, showing a reading of "90 mg/dL," labeled as "START: Homeostasis (70-110 mg/dL)." A pathway branches to the left, indicating a drop in blood glucose to "50 mg/dL," identified as "Hypoglycemia (low blood glucose)." This low blood glucose triggers "Glucagon release," where "Alpha cells of pancreas release glucagon," as shown in a detailed diagram of pancreatic islets with alpha cells and a splenic artery. An arrow from this box points to a section detailing "Glucagon effects." These effects include: "Inhibits body cells from taking up glucose from the blood and utilizing it in cellular respiration" (shown with a muscle cell diagram), "Stimulates glycogenolysis - glycogen in the liver is broken down into glucose and released into the blood" (shown with a liver diagram), and "Stimulates gluconeogenesis - amino acids and free glycerol are converted to glucose in the ER and released into the blood" (shown with diagrams of rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum). All these effects lead to an increase in "Blood glucose concentration," with an arrow pointing up from the "Glucagon effects" box to a box labeled "Blood glucose concentration increases." Finally, an arrow from this box points back to the "START: Homeostasis" state, completing the feedback loop that restores blood glucose to the homeostatic range of 70-110 mg/dL.

The video segment displays a diagram titled "THE ENDOCRINE PANCREAS" with the OpenStax logo in the top right corner. The diagram illustrates the process of insulin release and its effects. On the left, a box labeled "Insulin release:" shows an anatomical cross-section of a pancreas with beta cells (small, blue, circular structures) releasing insulin (represented by tiny blue dots) into a splenic artery (a red vessel). The text within this box states "• Beta cells of pancreas release insulin". Below this illustration, a digital blood glucose meter is depicted, showing a reading of "160 mg/dL," with the accompanying text "Hyperglycemia (elevated blood glucose)." An upward arrow points from this meter to the "Insulin release" box, signifying that hyperglycemia triggers insulin release. The overall background of the video is white with colorful horizontal and vertical stripes on the left and bottom edges.

The video segment presents an animated infographic explaining "DIABETES MELLITUS," displayed in green text at the top left of the screen, with a blue outlined circle at the top right. The main diagram central to the screen shows an internal organ, likely the pancreas, releasing small white glucose particles into a red blood vessel. Within this blood vessel, numerous white cube-like "Glucose" particles and fewer blue spherical "Insulin" particles are depicted flowing. A legend at the bottom left explicitly identifies these particles. Initially, a circular inset labeled "NORMAL CONDITION" is visible at the top right, illustrating a cell membrane with receptor proteins. Blue insulin particles are shown binding to these receptors, which then open channels, allowing white glucose particles to enter the cell. Around the 00:04 mark, additional text appears on the left side of the screen, stating: "Type 1:" followed by "Not enough insulin produced by pancreas. Most likely caused by autoimmune destruction of beta cells." Concurrently, a second circular inset appears at the bottom right, labeled "TYPE 1 DIABETES." This inset shows a similar cell membrane with receptors, but notably, no blue insulin particles are binding to them, resulting in closed channels and thus preventing white glucose particles from entering the cell. The narrator's voice describes diabetes mellitus as a disease resulting from "elevated blood glucose levels when insulin signaling is impaired."

The video displays a static medical illustration explaining Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus. The top left corner features the bold green title "DIABETES MELLITUS" followed by "Type 1:" and the explanation: "Not enough insulin produced by pancreas. Most likely caused by autoimmune destruction of beta cells." The main image shows a red blood vessel traversing cellular tissue, containing numerous small white square particles labeled "Glucose" and fewer tiny blue circular particles labeled "Insulin" (according to a legend at the bottom left). An inset on the far left shows a stomach-like organ, representing the pancreas, with glucose particles inside and a few insulin particles being secreted into the blood vessel. On the right, two circular insets provide magnified views of cell membranes. The top right inset, labeled "NORMAL CONDITION," illustrates blue insulin particles binding to brown X-shaped receptors on the cell membrane, which in turn open purple channels, allowing white glucose particles to enter the cell. Below it, the bottom right inset, labeled "TYPE 1 DIABETES," depicts the same cell membrane and receptors but with no insulin particles present to bind, resulting in closed channels and glucose particles unable to enter the cell. The entire illustration is framed by a colorful striped border, and a blue ring symbol, commonly used for diabetes awareness, is prominently displayed in the top right corner. A website link is visible at the bottom left for the image source.

The video frame displays a slide titled "DIABETES MELLITUS" in bold green text at the top left. Below this, "Type 1:" is written in bold, followed by two bullet points explaining Type 1 diabetes: "Not enough insulin produced by pancreas." and "Most likely caused by autoimmune destruction of beta cells." A blue circle icon is positioned in the top right corner. The main part of the slide features a detailed medical illustration. On the left, an inset shows a stomach-like organ, which is the pancreas, releasing small white squares (labeled "Glucose" in the legend) and blue circles (labeled "Insulin"). A blue arrow indicates these substances moving into a blood vessel. The blood vessel, depicted as a red tube, contains numerous white square-shaped glucose molecules and fewer blue circular insulin molecules. On the right side, two circular insets illustrate cellular activity. The top inset, labeled "NORMAL CONDITION," shows a cell membrane with purple and orange receptor proteins. Blue insulin molecules are binding to the orange receptors, allowing white glucose molecules to enter the cell through the purple channels. The bottom inset, labeled "TYPE 1 DIABETES," shows a similar cell membrane, but there are no blue insulin molecules binding to the receptors, and consequently, the white glucose molecules remain outside the cell. The entire slide has a colorful border with yellow, green, red, and blue blocks, and a web address "http://www.scientificanimations.com/wiki-images/" is visible at the bottom left.

The video displays a static image illustrating Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus. At the top left, the title "DIABETES MELLITUS" is written in green, with "Type 1:" highlighted in bold, followed by the description: "Not enough insulin produced by pancreas. Most likely caused by autoimmune destruction of beta cells." To the right of this text, a large blue outline of a circle is visible. The main part of the image features a reddish blood vessel running through a beige, cellular-like background, with white square-shaped glucose molecules and small blue circular insulin molecules flowing through it. An arrow indicates the path of these molecules. On the left, an inset image shows a human organ, likely the pancreas, surrounded by a stomach, with glucose molecules visible. On the right, two circular insets compare cellular activity: the top one, labeled "NORMAL CONDITION," shows insulin molecules (blue circles) binding to receptors (brown Y-shapes) on cell surfaces, allowing glucose (white squares) to enter the cell. The bottom inset, labeled "TYPE 1 DIABETES," shows fewer insulin molecules and glucose remaining outside the cells, as receptors are not activated. A legend at the bottom left clarifies that white squares represent "Glucose" and blue circles represent "Insulin." At the very bottom, a URL "http://www.scientificanimations.com/wiki-images/" is printed.

The video segment presents a detailed animated diagram illustrating Diabetes Mellitus, specifically Type 1. At the top left, the text "DIABETES MELLITUS" is displayed in green, followed by "Type 1: Not enough insulin produced by pancreas. Most likely caused by autoimmune destruction of beta cells." in black. A blue circle graphic is positioned in the top right corner. The main image features an internal view of the human body, with a red blood vessel running horizontally across the center. To the left, a stomach and pancreas are visible, with small white particles (labeled "Glucose" in the legend below) shown inside the stomach and being released from the pancreas. Blue spheres (labeled "Insulin" in the legend) are also seen originating from the pancreas and entering the blood vessel. Within the blood vessel, white cube-shaped glucose molecules and blue spherical insulin molecules are depicted, with an arrow indicating insulin moving into the vessel. Two circular insets are shown on the right side. The top inset, labeled "NORMAL CONDITION," illustrates a cell membrane with two brown, protein-like receptors. A blue insulin molecule is bound to one receptor, triggering the opening of a channel through which white glucose particles are actively entering the cell. The bottom inset, labeled "TYPE 1 DIABETES," shows a similar cell membrane and receptors, but no insulin molecules are bound, and the glucose particles remain outside the cell, unable to enter. The background of the main image depicts a cellular tissue structure. A URL "http://www.scientificanimations.com/wiki-images/" is visible at the very bottom. The video then transitions to a closer view of the cell membrane, focusing on the receptors.

The video frame at 00:03 displays a white slide titled "DIABETES MELLITUS" in bold green letters, with "Type 2:" in black text below it. The accompanying descriptive text reads: "Cells throughout the body do not respond to insulin (insulin insensitivity). Initially a normal (or even elevated) amount of insulin is produced but cells don't respond. Over time pancreas may stop producing insulin." Below this text is a detailed illustration of a cell membrane, composed of a double layer of small, reddish-brown circular structures. Several larger, irregularly shaped protein channels are embedded within this membrane. On the far left, a brown channel protein is shown with a small blue sphere (representing insulin) attached to its top, and small white particles (likely glucose) are depicted moving through it into the cell. Next to it, a pink channel protein also shows white particles flowing through an open channel. Further right, another brown-yellow channel protein, also with a blue sphere attached, allows white particles to enter. However, the last channel protein on the far right, which is purple, appears closed and is not allowing any white particles to pass through, illustrating cellular insensitivity. In the top right corner, a blue circle with a white interior, the international symbol for diabetes, is displayed. The entire slide is framed by a colorful border with segments of green, red, orange, and yellow. A small caption at the bottom left reads: "http://www.scientificanimations.com/wiki-images/".

The video segment opens with a slide featuring the title "COMPLICATIONS OF DIABETES MELLITUS" in green text at the top. The main part of the slide displays three distinct medical illustrations against a light blue-grey background. On the left, there is a circular image depicting the retina of an eye, characterized by a network of red blood vessels, with several visible white and red spots indicating damage or hemorrhages, representing diabetic retinopathy. In the center, a human kidney is shown, appearing shrunken, discolored, and irregular in shape, suggestive of advanced kidney disease or diabetic nephropathy. On the right, a human foot is depicted, and next to it, three yellow, elongated structures, representing nerves, are shown in a progressive state of deterioration from top to bottom, illustrating diabetic neuropathy. At the very bottom of the slide, a URL "http://www.scientificanimations.com/wiki-images/" is visible in small print. The entire slide is framed by a colorful border consisting of vertical stripes (yellow, orange, red, green, blue) on the sides and horizontal stripes at the top and bottom.

The video displays a static image titled "COMPLICATIONS OF DIABETES MELLITUS" in green text against a white background, framed by a colorful border of yellow, orange, green, and blue stripes. Below the title, three medical illustrations are presented on a light grey background. On the left, a circular image depicts a red human retina with visible blood vessels, some appearing dilated or hemorrhagic, indicative of diabetic retinopathy. In the center, a discolored, irregularly shaped organ, likely a kidney, appears damaged or diseased, representing diabetic nephropathy. On the right, a human foot is shown next to three cross-sectional diagrams of nerves. The top nerve diagram appears healthy, while the middle and bottom ones show progressive damage to the nerve's outer layer (myelin sheath), illustrating diabetic neuropathy. At the very bottom of the screen, a small URL "http://www.scientificanimations.com/wiki-images/" is visible.

The video segment displays a slide titled "COMPLICATIONS OF DIABETES MELLITUS" in green text against a light blue-grey background, framed by a colorful, striped border. The slide features three distinct medical illustrations. On the left, a circular image depicts the retina of an eye, characterized by a dense network of red blood vessels and several bright white spots, signifying potential damage due to diabetic retinopathy. In the center, a human kidney is illustrated, appearing enlarged, discolored with brown and purple hues, and having an uneven, textured surface, indicative of diabetic nephropathy. To the right, a human foot with visible toes is shown, next to which are three yellow, elongated, segmented structures resembling nerves. These structures appear to thin towards their ends, suggesting damage or degeneration often associated with diabetic neuropathy. There are no people visible in this segment.
